pages.description: Back-of-the-envelope estimation cheatsheet: the numbers to memorise, an animated sizing of a real service, the latency ladder scaled to human time, peak factors, Little's Law and cost anchors.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The power of ten an answer sits at. Getting that right is the whole job; the leading digit is a bonus.
terms.detail: The question an estimate answers is never "what exactly is it" but "which regime are we in", because each regime has a different right answer. Scale What it implies < 100 QPS one machine, one database, no cache. Stop designing. 100–1,000 QPS a few instances behind a load balancer, one database with an index review 1,000–10,000 QPS caching matters, read replicas, connection pooling becomes the bottleneck 10,000–100,000 QPS sharding, CDN, async everything, a dedicated capacity story > 100,000 QPS a different architecture and a different team size < 1 TB total fits on one machine; "big data" tooling is a liability here > 100 TB storage cost is now a product decision, not an infrastructure one Being off by 2x rarely changes the regime. Being off by 100x always does — and that is the error an estimate is designed to catch, usually in the first two minutes.

terms.def: Round every input to one significant figure, preferably to a power of ten, before multiplying. Precision you did not have is precision you cannot keep.
terms.detail: Rounding is not sloppiness; it is what makes the arithmetic doable in your head, and errors in opposite directions cancel as you multiply. Awkward Use Error 86,400 s/day 100,000 +16%, and it rounds toward safety on QPS 365 days 400, or 300 for a lower bound ±10% 1,024 1,000 2.4% 31,536,000 s/year 3 x 10^7 (or π x 10^7) < 5% 7,300 QPS 10,000 +37%, and far easier to carry Two habits worth building. Work in powers of ten and keep the exponent separate: 2 x 10^7 x 5 x 10^3 = 10 x 10^10 = 10^11. And when an input is genuinely uncertain, do the calculation twice with your optimistic and pessimistic guesses — if both land in the same regime, you are done. Finally, round in the direction that would hurt. If overestimating load is safer than underestimating it, round up.

terms.def: Queries per second: daily volume divided by 86,400. The number almost every other number is derived from.
terms.detail: The conversion is one division, and the trick is to use 100,000 seconds per day so you can do it by shifting a decimal point. 1,000,000 requests/day -> 10 QPS 100,000,000 /day -> 1,000 QPS 1,000,000,000 /day -> 10,000 QPS Rough anchors QPS A busy internal line-of-business app 10–100 A popular SaaS product 1,000–10,000 A large consumer app 100,000+ One modest API instance can serve 500–2,000 (simple JSON, cached) One Postgres instance, simple indexed reads 5,000–20,000 One Redis instance 100,000+ Always split reads from writes. The ratio between them decides more of the architecture than the absolute number does — 250:1 means caching and replicas, while 1:1 means the write path is your problem.

terms.def: Traffic is never flat. Multiply the average by 2–4 for a normal daily peak, and far more for an event.
terms.detail: Average QPS is a billing number. Peak QPS is a capacity number, and they are not interchangeable. Why the average line is not the number you provision Workload Peak / average Consumer app, global audience 2–3x Consumer app, single country 3–5x B2B, office hours in one timezone 4–6x Batch or cron-driven 10–100x — it is all peak Flash sale, ticket drop, TV moment 20–100x Above roughly 10x, stop provisioning for the peak: it is cheaper to queue, shed or rate-limit. That is a design decision the estimate just made for you.

terms.def: The ladder from L1 cache to an intercontinental round trip. Knowing the rungs stops you designing something physics forbids.
terms.detail: Approximate, current-hardware values. The exact figures matter far less than the ratios, which have been stable for years. Operation Time vs L1 L1 cache reference ~1 ns 1x Branch mispredict ~3 ns 3x L2 cache reference ~4 ns 4x Mutex lock / unlock, uncontended ~20 ns 20x Main memory reference ~100 ns 100x Compress 1 KB (fast codec) ~2 µs 2,000x Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM ~50 µs 50,000x NVMe SSD random read (4 KB) ~20 µs 20,000x Round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms 500,000x Read 1 MB sequentially from NVMe ~0.3 ms 300,000x Spinning-disk seek ~5 ms 5,000,000x Round trip, same continent ~20 ms — Round trip, Europe to California ~150 ms — Three rules fall out of this table and cover most design arguments: memory is ~100x faster than an SSD, a network hop costs more than a local disk read, and the speed of light sets a floor nobody can buy their way past — only a copy nearer the user can. The light-speed floor is worth computing once: light does about 200 km/ms in fibre, so London to New York (5,600 km) is 28 ms one way and 56 ms round trip at best. Real paths are not straight; 70–90 ms is typical.

terms.def: Bytes per field, per row, per object. Estimate by adding up what is actually stored, then double it for overhead.
terms.detail: Most storage estimates fail on this line, usually by forgetting indexes. Thing Size int / bigint 4 / 8 B UUID (binary / text) 16 / 36 B Timestamp 8 B Short text field (name, email) 20–60 B Typical relational row 100–1,000 B JSON document 1–10 KB Log line 200 B–2 KB Web page (HTML only) 50–200 KB Phone photo 2–5 MB Minute of 1080p video ~50 MB Embedding vector (1,536 x float32) 6 KB Multipliers you will forget Indexes: add 20–100% of the table size. A table with five indexes can be larger than its data. Replication: x2 or x3, before backups. Backups and snapshots: often another x1–2 over the retention period. Compression: divide by 3–10 for text and logs, by 1 for already-compressed media. Rule of thumb: whatever you computed, multiply by three. You will be closer than if you did not.

terms.def: Daily volume times retention times replication. The number that most often kills a design, and the one most often left out of it.
terms.detail: Storage is the only resource that accumulates. CPU and bandwidth reset every second; bytes written in January are still being paid for in December. total = items/day x bytes/item x retention_days x replicas x (1 + index_overhead) Example Per day Per year Audit log: 10M events x 500 B 5 GB 1.8 TB App logs: 100M lines x 1 KB 100 GB 36 TB Photos: 20M x 2 MB 40 TB 15 PB Metrics: 10k series x 1 point/10 s x 16 B 1.4 GB 500 GB Two questions turn an unaffordable number into an affordable one: how long must we really keep it, and does it have to stay hot. Dropping log retention from 365 to 30 days is a 12x saving, and archival storage is 5–10x cheaper than hot. Always project three to five years, not one. A design that is fine at year one and impossible at year three is a design you will rewrite under pressure.

terms.def: QPS multiplied by payload size. Convert to bits per second before comparing with any network specification.
terms.detail: The conversion that trips everyone: network links are specified in bits, storage and payloads in bytes. One factor of eight, applied in the wrong direction, is an 64x error. Link Bytes per second 1 Gbps 125 MB/s 10 Gbps 1.25 GB/s 25 Gbps 3.1 GB/s 100 Gbps 12.5 GB/s 50,000 reads/s x 200 KB = 10 GB/s = 80 Gbps # needs a CDN, not a server 1,000 reads/s x 20 KB = 20 MB/s = 160 Mbps # one ordinary instance Useful anchors: a single modern server does 10–25 Gbps comfortably; anything that needs more than roughly 10 Gbps of user-facing egress belongs behind a CDN, and the egress bill will become one of your top three cloud line items long before the bandwidth becomes a technical problem. Also check the time dimension: moving 100 TB over a 10 Gbps link takes about a day of saturated transfer. For a migration, that is the number that decides whether you ship disks instead.

terms.def: concurrency = arrival rate x latency. Three quantities; know two and the third is determined. It sizes pools and queues.
terms.detail: The most useful formula in capacity planning, and the one that explains why a service with plenty of CPU still falls over. L = λ x W concurrent_requests = requests_per_second x seconds_per_request Rate Latency Concurrency needed 1,000 /s 10 ms 10 1,000 /s 100 ms 100 1,000 /s 1 s 1,000 threads or connections 100 /s 2 s 200 Read that third row carefully: nothing about the request rate changed, but a tenfold latency increase demands a thousand concurrent slots. This is exactly what happens when a dependency slows down, and why a pool sized for the happy path exhausts itself during an incident. Run it backwards too. A connection pool of 100 against a database with 20 ms queries can sustain 100 / 0.02 = 5,000 queries per second — and not one more, whatever the CPU graph says.

terms.def: How many reads per write. The single number that decides most of the architecture before any other consideration.
terms.detail: Ratios cluster, and each cluster has a standard answer. Ratio Example Implication 1000:1 news site, product catalogue cache almost everything; the write path is irrelevant 100:1 social feed, e-commerce heavy caching, read replicas, precompute on write 10:1 typical business app ordinary caching, one primary is usually fine 1:1 chat, collaborative editing the write path is the design; caching helps little 1:100 telemetry, IoT ingestion append-only storage, batching, a log, time-series database Estimate it from behaviour, not from the database. "Each user posts twice and scrolls past 200 posts" gives you 100:1 directly, and that is enough to know whether the conversation should be about caching or about ingest. It also tells you where to spend effort: at 1000:1, halving read cost is worth a thousand times more than halving write cost.

terms.def: Not all data is accessed equally. Usually around 20% of it serves 80% of requests, and recent data dominates.
terms.detail: This is what makes caching work at all, and what makes storage affordable: you only need the hot slice to be fast. Pattern Typical shape Social feed 90% of reads touch data from the last 24 hours E-commerce catalogue top 5% of products get 60–80% of views Logs and metrics 99% of queries are over the last 7 days Document archive almost all reads in the first week, then near zero Sizing a cache follows directly: cache the hot slice, not the dataset. For 200 PB of photos where 1% is hot, roughly 2 TB of cache plus a CDN buys an excellent hit ratio — and the caching strategies page covers how to choose the TTLs and eviction policy that keep it that way. The same split drives tiering: hot on SSD, warm on object storage, cold on archival. A 5–10x price difference between tiers applied to 95% of your bytes is usually the largest single cost saving available.

terms.def: Peak load divided by what one machine does, plus headroom. The last step before the number becomes money.
terms.detail: Per-machine capacity is the input people most often guess badly, so anchor it rather than imagining it. Workload One modern instance handles Static files / reverse proxy 50,000–100,000 req/s Simple JSON API, cached 2,000–10,000 req/s API with a database round trip 500–2,000 req/s Heavy computation / rendering 10–100 req/s Postgres, simple indexed reads 5,000–20,000 QPS Redis, single instance 100,000+ ops/s Kafka broker 100 MB/s+ sustained machines = peak_qps / per_machine_qps / target_utilisation = 150,000 / 1,000 / 0.5 = 300 If the answer is under 5, do not design a distributed system: build one service, run three for availability, and revisit when the number changes. If the answer is over 1,000, the interesting question is no longer "how many" but "what else is wrong" — at that scale, cost per request usually dominates the architecture.

terms.def: The gap between what you provision and what you use. Running a system at 90% utilisation is a decision to have no response to anything.
terms.detail: Headroom pays for the things an estimate cannot model: a deploy, an instance failure, an unexpectedly popular feature, a retry storm. Target utilisation Suitable for 30–40% stateful systems, slow-scaling tiers, anything where failover doubles a neighbour's load 50–60% typical stateless services — the usual default 70–80% fast-autoscaling, well-understood workloads > 85% batch jobs that can wait, and nothing else The subtle one is N+1 across a pool: with three instances at 60%, losing one puts the other two at 90%, and they fall over too. With five at 60%, losing one puts the rest at 75%. The smaller the pool, the more headroom each member needs. Queues need headroom in time, not capacity: a queue that drains exactly as fast as it fills has infinite latency the moment anything hiccups. Aim for a consumer that can drain at 2–3x the arrival rate.

terms.def: Rough unit prices, good to a factor of two. Enough to tell whether an idea is cheap, expensive or impossible.
terms.detail: Approximate cloud list prices. Vary by provider, region and commitment — but for a decision, "about $0.02 per GB-month" is all you need. Resource Rough price Object storage, hot $0.02 / GB / month Object storage, archive $0.002 / GB / month Block storage (SSD) $0.08–0.12 / GB / month Managed database storage $0.10–0.25 / GB / month Egress to the internet $0.05–0.09 / GB CDN egress $0.01–0.04 / GB General-purpose VM (4 vCPU, 16 GB) $100–150 / month on demand Same, 1–3 year commitment 30–60% less Two anchors worth memorising because they decide so many arguments: 1 PB of hot object storage is roughly $20,000 per month, and 1 PB of internet egress is roughly $50,000. Once you know those, "we'll just store all of it and serve it from origin" stops being a design and becomes a budget request. Compare against the business, not against other infrastructure. $4M a month is cheap for a product with $100M of revenue and fatal for one with $2M.

terms.def: The last step, and the one people skip: compare the answer with something you already know to be true.
terms.detail: An estimate without a sanity check is a number with no error bars and no defence. Check Question Dimensional do the units actually produce the thing I asked for? Human does this imply every person on Earth does it four times a day? Hardware does this imply a disk faster than any disk? Known system is this larger than a company I know to be much larger than us? Money is this more than the revenue of the product? Dimensional analysis alone catches most arithmetic slips. If you are computing servers and the units come out as "requests per second per byte", you inverted something — and you would never have noticed from the digits. The strongest check is a known reference point. If your estimate of a national bank's daily transactions exceeds the number of card transactions in the world, something is wrong by about a thousand, and knowing that is more useful than any refinement of the inputs.

terms.def: Which assumption dominates the answer. Find it, and spend your remaining time on that one input only.
terms.detail: In a chain of multiplications, the input with the widest uncertainty controls the output. Everything else is noise you do not need to refine. In the photo-service estimate, the inputs are 100M users (known within 20%), 0.2 uploads per user (a guess, possibly 5x off), 2 MB per photo (known within 2x), 5-year retention (a policy choice) and 3 replicas (a design choice). The uploads per user dominates: get it wrong by 5x and the 200 PB becomes 40 PB or 1 EB, and the conclusion flips. Technique How High / low pass run the estimate with optimistic and pessimistic inputs; if both land in the same regime, stop Vary one input double each input in turn and see which moves the answer most Name the dominant term state it out loud: "this whole thing hinges on uploads per user" This is also the honest way to present an estimate. "Somewhere between 40 and 400 PB, driven almost entirely by how often people actually upload — and we can measure that in a week" is a far more useful sentence than a single confident number.

pages.title: Caching strategies
pages.tagline: Keep the answer near the question — and decide, up front, how wrong you are willing to be.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · patterns are timeless; the examples are .NET 9+, Redis and HTTP
pages.description: Caching strategies cheatsheet: cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind and refresh-ahead, with animated walk-throughs of write paths, stampedes and invalidation races.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The fraction of lookups answered by the cache. It decides the average latency and, more importantly, how much load reaches the thing behind it.
terms.detail: Hit ratio is the number that turns a cache from a vibe into a measurement. Average latency is hit_ratio x hit_cost + (1 − hit_ratio) x miss_cost, and the miss cost usually dominates. What the numbers actually mean Hit ratio Avg latency (1 ms hit, 50 ms miss) Load reaching the DB 50% 25.5 ms half of it 90% 5.9 ms 1 in 10 99% 1.5 ms 1 in 100 99.9% 1.05 ms 1 in 1,000 Two consequences people miss. First, going from 90% to 99% halves the backend load again — the marginal value of hit ratio grows as it approaches 1. Second, a system tuned to run comfortably at a 99% hit ratio is running at 100x its sustainable load if the cache ever empties, which is why a cold cache after a deploy or a flush can take the database down. Measure hits, misses and evictions separately. A falling hit ratio with rising evictions means the cache is too small; a falling hit ratio with stable evictions means your keys have too much cardinality or your TTLs are too short.

terms.def: Also "lazy loading". Your code checks the cache, and on a miss reads the source and populates the cache itself. The cache knows nothing about the database.
terms.detail: The default pattern, and the one in almost every codebase. The application owns the whole flow: var cached = await cache.GetAsync(key); if (cached is not null) return cached; // hit var value = await db.LoadProductAsync(42); // miss: go to the source await cache.SetAsync(key, value, ttl: 5min); // populate for next time return value; Property Consequence Only requested data is cached no wasted memory on cold items Cache and DB models can differ cache the rendered DTO, not the row A cache outage is survivable every call just becomes a miss — if the DB can take it Every miss pays double a failed lookup plus the real query Writes are your problem you must invalidate, and the race is real Pair it with write-side invalidation (delete the key, do not update it) and a TTL as a backstop for the invalidations you will inevitably miss.

terms.def: The cache sits in front of the source and loads missing entries itself. Your code only ever talks to the cache.
terms.detail: Same read path as cache-aside, but the "go and fetch it" logic lives in the cache library rather than in each call site. In .NET, HybridCache.GetOrCreateAsync is exactly this. // the factory is only invoked on a miss, and only once per key var product = await hybridCache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}", async ct => await db.LoadProductAsync(id, ct), new HybridCacheEntryOptions { Expiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5) }); Why prefer it over hand-rolled cache-aside One implementation instead of one per call site, so the TTL, the serializer and the metrics are consistent. Stampede protection comes for free: concurrent callers for the same key await the same task. Caching a null result (negative caching) is handled once rather than forgotten everywhere. The cost is coupling: your cache now needs to know how to load your data, which makes a cache library harder to swap and makes the loader's failures look like cache failures.

terms.def: Writes go to the cache and to the source synchronously, before the caller is acknowledged. Cache and database never disagree.
terms.detail: The write path mirrors read-through: the cache is the only thing your code talks to, and it forwards the write to the source before returning. Property Effect Consistency strong between cache and source — no stale window Write latency cache write plus full source write (the slower of the two) Durability same as the database: nothing is acknowledged before it is committed Cache contents everything written, whether or not anyone reads it The hidden cost is that last row: a write-heavy, read-light table fills the cache with entries nobody ever reads, evicting the ones people do. Combine write-through with a short TTL, or use write-around for data that is written far more often than it is read. See the first animation for the full write path, and what changes when the same write becomes write-behind.

terms.def: Also "write-back". The write is acknowledged as soon as the cache holds it, and flushed to the source later, usually in batches.
terms.detail: The fastest write path and the only one that can lose data. The cache acknowledges, buffers the change as dirty, and a background flush writes it to the source after a delay or when a batch fills. Knob Typical What it buys Flush interval 100 ms – 5 s batching; longer means fewer, larger writes Batch size 100 – 10,000 rows amortises round trips and index maintenance Data-loss window = flush interval exactly what you lose if the node dies It wins when the same key is written repeatedly — a view counter hit 10,000 times a minute becomes one UPDATE instead of 10,000 — or when the source is slow and the write is not the user's last word on the subject. Never use it for data you cannot reconstruct: payments, orders, audit logs. "We lost 400 ms of writes" is an acceptable sentence about page-view counters and an unacceptable one about money. If you need both speed and durability, write to an append-only log such as Apache Kafka and project into the database asynchronously — same shape, but the buffer is durable.

terms.def: Writes go straight to the source and simply invalidate (or skip) the cache. The entry is only populated when somebody actually reads it.
terms.detail: The quiet default for cache-aside systems: on a write, DELETE the key rather than updating it, and let the next reader repopulate. await db.UpdatePriceAsync(42, 79); await cache.RemoveAsync("product:42"); // not Set — see the invalidation race Compared to Difference write-through does not pollute the cache with write-only data; first read after a write is a miss updating the key in place avoids writing a value you computed from a row you may have read before someone else's write Delete, do not update. A delete is idempotent and always safe; a set can write a stale value computed moments ago, and that value then survives until its TTL. The invalidation deep dive animates exactly how that goes wrong.

terms.def: Refresh popular entries before they expire, in the background, so that no user request ever pays for a miss.
terms.detail: Two flavours. Proactive: a scheduled job recomputes a known set of hot keys on a timer. Probabilistic: on each read, refresh early with a probability that rises as the entry nears expiry — the "XFetch" trick. # refresh early, with increasing probability as the TTL runs out if now - delta * beta * log(random()) >= expiry: refresh_in_background(key) return cached_value Use it for Not for a small, known set of hot keys (homepage, pricing, feature flags) long-tail keys — you would refresh millions of entries nobody wants values that are expensive to compute (reports, aggregations) values that change unpredictably: refresh-ahead still serves the previous one The cost is wasted work: you recompute entries that might never be read again. That is a good trade for the top 100 keys and a terrible one for the next million.

terms.def: Time to live: how long an entry may be served before it is discarded. The simplest, most robust correctness backstop you have.
terms.detail: A TTL is an admission that your invalidation will sometimes fail. It bounds the damage: however badly the invalidation goes, the wrong value disappears within the TTL. Common values Data TTL Why Static assets (hashed filename) 1 year, immutable the name changes when the content does Product catalogue 5–60 min changes rarely, staleness is cheap Prices, stock levels 10–60 s wrong values cost money User session / permissions 1–15 min a revoked permission must not linger Feature flags 5–30 s a kill switch must actually kill Expensive report 1–24 h cost dominates freshness Negative result (not found) 5–30 s short, so a newly created item appears quickly Always add jitter: ttl = base + random(0, base * 0.1). Entries created together — by a deploy, a warm-up script or a bulk import — otherwise expire together and produce a synchronised stampede. Distinguish absolute expiry (dies at a fixed time, predictable) from sliding expiry (extends on each access, keeps hot items alive but can keep a stale value alive forever). Most caches, including .NET's HybridCache, let you set both: a sliding window with an absolute cap.

terms.def: What gets thrown out when the cache is full: least recently used, least frequently used, FIFO, or something smarter. Eviction is not expiry.
terms.detail: Expiry is about correctness (this value is too old); eviction is about capacity (I need the space). A key can disappear for either reason, and your code must handle both identically. Policy Keeps Weak against LRU recently touched entries a scan: one bulk job evicts your whole working set LFU frequently touched entries changing popularity; yesterday's hot key will not leave FIFO nothing in particular almost everything; simple but rarely best W-TinyLFU frequency with a recency window little — it is the modern default (Caffeine, many CDNs) noeviction everything; writes fail instead use for queues and primary data, never for a cache In Redis the choice is maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, volatile-lru when the same instance also holds data that must not vanish. Watch evicted_keys — a non-zero and rising number means your cache is too small for its working set, and your hit ratio is paying for it.

terms.def: Removing or replacing an entry because the underlying data changed. The hard half of caching, and the source of the subtlest bugs.
terms.detail: Three strategies, in increasing order of effort and precision: Strategy Precision Effort TTL only coarse: wrong for up to the TTL none Explicit delete on write good, if you find every write path medium, and easy to miss one Event-driven (CDC, outbox, change feed) high: the database itself tells you high, but it catches writes your code did not make Tag-based invalidation ("drop everything tagged product:42 ") is what you want once one entity appears in many cached views — a product page, a category listing and a search result all go stale from one price change. HybridCache.RemoveByTagAsync and CDN surrogate keys both do this. The cache-aside invalidation race Note the shape of the bug: nobody did anything wrong, the operations were individually correct, and the window is a few milliseconds wide. At 5,000 requests per second, a few milliseconds happens constantly.

terms.def: Also "dogpile" or "thundering herd". A hot key expires and every concurrent request misses at once, hitting the source with the full, uncached load.
terms.detail: The counter-intuitive part: the better your hit ratio, the worse the stampede, because the source has been sized for the trickle it normally sees. The four fixes, in order of preference Fix How it works Cost Single-flight / lock one request recomputes, the rest await the same task the waiters still wait once Stale-while-revalidate serve the expired value, refresh in the background a bounded extra staleness Probabilistic early refresh recompute before expiry with rising probability some wasted recomputation TTL jitter spreads expiry so keys do not die together none — always do this In .NET, HybridCache gives you single-flight within an instance and across the distributed layer without extra code, which is the main reason to prefer it over a hand-written IDistributedCache wrapper. In Python or Go, a mutex keyed on the cache key does the same job for the in-process layer; a Redis SET NX lock covers the fleet. The second animation on this page walks through the failure and both fixes.

terms.def: Serve the expired value immediately and refresh it in the background. Latency stays flat; the price is a bounded window of known staleness.
terms.detail: An entry gets two lifetimes: fresh (serve without thinking) and stale but usable (serve, then refresh behind the scenes). It is the single most effective trick for keeping p99 latency flat. Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400 Directive Means max-age=60 fresh for 60 s stale-while-revalidate=300 for the next 300 s, serve the old copy and refresh in the background stale-if-error=86400 if the origin is down, keep serving the old copy for a day stale-if-error deserves special mention: it turns your CDN into a last line of defence that keeps the site readable through a complete backend outage. It costs one header. Do not use it where staleness is a correctness bug — account balances, stock levels at checkout, permissions after a revocation.

terms.def: Caching the fact that something does not exist, so that repeated lookups for missing keys do not hammer the source.
terms.detail: Without it, every request for a non-existent id is a guaranteed miss, and an attacker who enumerates random ids gets a direct line to your database — a cache penetration attack. Technique Use when Cache a sentinel "not found" with a short TTL (5–30 s) always, as a baseline Bloom filter in front of the cache huge keyspace, many legitimate misses Validate the key shape before looking it up ids with a checksum or known format — free and effective Keep negative TTLs much shorter than positive ones: a user who just signed up should not be told "no such account" for five minutes because a page load beat the write. Be careful to distinguish "the source says it does not exist" from "the source timed out". Caching the second one turns a blip into a sustained outage.

terms.def: Several caches in series — browser, CDN, in-process, distributed — each with its own hit ratio, TTL and invalidation story.
terms.detail: Latency per layer is what makes the hierarchy worth the complexity. The numbers below are the ones worth memorising: The trap is invalidation across layers. Deleting a key in Redis does nothing to the copy sitting in 40 process-local caches, so an in-process layer needs either a very short TTL (5–30 s) or a broadcast channel. .NET's HybridCache handles both tiers and propagates tag invalidation; Redis pub/sub or key-space notifications do it by hand. Rule: the further a layer is from the source, the shorter its TTL must be, because its invalidation is less reliable.

terms.def: The cache has no schema, so the key naming convention is the schema. It decides cardinality, invalidation granularity and hit ratio.
terms.detail: Include everything that changes the value, and nothing that does not. Each extra dimension multiplies the number of entries and divides the hit ratio. Key Verdict product:42:v3 good — the v3 lets a schema change invalidate everything at once product:42:en-GB:eur good if the rendered value really differs by locale and currency search:{query}:{page}:{sort}:{userId} bad — userId makes every entry unique; hit ratio near zero product:42:{requestId} catastrophic — unbounded cardinality, pure memory leak Normalise before hashing: sort query parameters, lowercase, drop tracking parameters such as utm_*. A CDN that treats ?utm_source=x as a distinct key caches your homepage a thousand times and hits none of them. Put a version segment in the prefix. When the serialized shape changes, bumping v3 to v4 invalidates everything instantly, with no scan and no risk of deserializing an old shape into a new type.

terms.def: How far the cached copy may drift from the source, and for how long. This is a product decision wearing a technical costume.
terms.detail: Every cache is eventually consistent. The only question is the size of the window and who pays when it is exceeded. Staleness budget Strategy that fits Zero (money, permissions at the point of use) do not cache, or write-through with explicit invalidation and read-your-writes Seconds short TTL + delete-on-write; stale-while-revalidate off Minutes cache-aside with a TTL, invalidation best-effort Hours refresh-ahead or a scheduled rebuild; serve stale on error Read-your-writes deserves its own line. A user who edits their profile and immediately sees the old version assumes the save failed and does it again. Fix it by invalidating synchronously on the write path, or by bypassing the cache for the writer for a few seconds (a cookie or a request-scoped flag), even when every other reader gets a cached copy. Write the budget down per data type, next to the TTL. A TTL with no stated budget is a number somebody picked once and nobody can safely change.

terms.def: The cache you get for free: Cache-Control, ETag and conditional requests, honoured by browsers, proxies and CDNs without any code.
terms.detail: Before adding a cache inside your application, check whether the response could simply be cacheable. The cheapest request is the one that never reaches your server. Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=600 ETag: "a3f9c1" Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language Directive Effect public / private may a shared cache (CDN, proxy) store it, or only the browser? max-age=N fresh for N seconds s-maxage=N a different, usually longer, freshness just for shared caches no-store never written to disk or memory — the one for personal data no-cache may be stored, but must be revalidated first (not the same as no-store) must-revalidate never serve stale once expired, even if the origin is unreachable With an ETag, a revalidation that finds nothing changed returns 304 Not Modified with no body — still a round trip, but a few hundred bytes instead of a few hundred kilobytes. Vary is the footgun. Vary: Cookie on a page served to logged-in users makes every entry unique and the cache useless; worse, getting Vary wrong on a public response can serve one user's page to another.

pages.title: Docker
pages.tagline: Package an app with everything it needs, then run it the same way on any machine.
pages.description: Docker cheatsheet: architecture, animated docker run and build-cache walk-throughs, key concepts, commands, trade-offs and alternatives.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A read-only template: a stack of filesystem layers plus metadata (start command, env vars, exposed ports). Built once, run anywhere.
terms.detail: An image is a list of layer tarballs plus a JSON config (entrypoint, env vars, working dir, exposed ports, user). It is immutable and identified by a content hash (digest). Typical base image sizes Base Size Notes alpine ~8 MB musl libc: some Python wheels must compile python:3.13-slim ~45 MB compressed Debian minimal, good default python:3.13 ~400 MB full toolchain, use as build stage distroless / chiseled ~20–50 MB no shell, smallest attack surface One image can target several CPU architectures (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) under the same tag: a multi-platform image.

terms.def: A running (or stopped) instance of an image: an isolated process with its own writable layer. Many containers can run from one image.
terms.detail: A container = image layers (read-only) + its own writable layer + runtime settings (env, ports, mounts, limits) + an isolated process. Lifecycle created → running → paused / exited → removed. A stopped container still exists (and keeps its writable layer) until docker rm. PID 1 inside the container is your app; when it exits, the container stops. Restart policies: --restart unless-stopped keeps services up across crashes and host reboots. Limit resources: --memory 512m --cpus 1.5.

terms.def: The filesystem changes made by one Dockerfile instruction. Layers are content-addressed, cached and shared between images.
terms.detail: Each filesystem-changing instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a layer containing only the files it added, changed or deleted. Layers are stacked with a union filesystem (overlayfs). Deleting a file in a later layer hides it but doesn't shrink the image: the bytes are still in the earlier layer. Clean up in the same RUN that created the files. Layers are shared: ten images on python:3.13-slim store the base once. Inspect with docker history myapp:1.0 or the dive tool.

terms.def: A text file of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD …) that describes how to build an image.
terms.detail: Instruction Does FROM base image (one per stage) WORKDIR set and create the working directory COPY / ADD add files from the build context (prefer COPY) RUN run a command at build time, creating a layer ENV / ARG runtime env var / build-time variable EXPOSE document the port (doesn't publish it) USER run as this user from here on CMD / ENTRYPOINT default command / fixed executable HEALTHCHECK command Docker runs to report health Order instructions from least to most frequently changing so the build cache helps you.

terms.def: Docker reuses a layer when its instruction and inputs are unchanged. Once one step changes, every later step is rebuilt.
terms.detail: For each instruction, BuildKit checks whether it already built the same instruction on the same parent layer with the same inputs (for COPY, a checksum of the copied files). If yes, it reuses the layer. The first cache miss invalidates every later step. RUN apt-get update is cached too, so combine it with install in one RUN. Cache mounts keep package caches between builds: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt. CI runners start empty; export the cache to a registry (--cache-to type=registry) or use the GitHub Actions cache. Force a clean build with --no-cache.

terms.def: A server that stores and distributes images: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, ECR, ACR, or a private one.
terms.detail: A registry stores images in repositories (ghcr.io/acme/web ), each with many tags. Pull and push use the OCI distribution API; only missing layers are transferred. Registry Notes Docker Hub default for unqualified names; pull rate limits for anonymous users GitHub Container Registry ghcr.io, permissions tied to the repo Azure ACR / AWS ECR / Google Artifact Registry close to your cloud workloads, private networking Harbor self-hosted, with scanning and replication Scan images for known vulnerabilities (Docker Scout, Trivy) as part of CI.

terms.def: nginx:1.27 is a movable tag; nginx@sha256:… is an immutable digest. Pin digests (or exact tags) in production.
terms.detail: nginx:1.27 is a tag: a human-friendly pointer that can be moved to a new image at any time. nginx@sha256:3b2f… is a digest: the hash of the image manifest, which can never change. latest is just the default tag name, not "the newest". Tag your builds with something unique: version (1.4.2) and/or git SHA (sha-9f3c2a1 ). Pin base images by digest in production Dockerfiles for fully reproducible builds; let a bot (Dependabot, Renovate) update the pin.

terms.def: Storage managed by Docker that lives outside the container's writable layer, so data survives when the container is removed.
terms.detail: docker volume create pgdata docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17 A named volume lives in Docker's storage area (/var/lib/docker/volumes ), independent of any container. Remove and recreate the container and the data is still there. Faster than bind mounts on Docker Desktop (stays inside the Linux VM). Back up by running a throwaway container: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/d -v .:/b alpine tar czf /b/pg.tgz -C /d.. docker compose down -v deletes the project's volumes. Careful.

terms.def: Maps a host folder into a container (-v ./src:/app ). Handy for live code reloading in development.
terms.detail: -v ./src:/app/src (or --mount type=bind,…) maps a host path into the container. Changes appear on both sides instantly, which is ideal for hot-reloading code in development. File ownership follows host UIDs, which can cause permission errors with non-root containers. On Windows and macOS, file I/O crosses the VM boundary and can be slow for large trees (node_modules ). Keep the repo inside WSL 2 on Windows. Add :ro to mount read-only. Use volumes for data, bind mounts for source code and config you edit.

terms.def: Virtual network for containers. On a user-defined bridge network, containers reach each other by name (http://api:8000 ).
terms.detail: Driver What it does bridge (default) private network on the host; NAT to the outside user-defined bridge same, plus DNS: containers reach each other by name host container shares the host network stack (Linux only) none no networking Compose creates a user-defined network per project, so api can call http://cache:6379. On the default bridge network, name resolution doesn't work: always create your own network.

terms.def: -p 8080:80 forwards host port 8080 to port 80 inside the container. Without it the service is unreachable from outside.
terms.detail: -p 8080:80 = host port 8080 → container port 80. Docker adds NAT rules on the host so traffic reaching 8080 is forwarded to the container's private IP. -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 binds only to localhost; plain -p 8080:80 listens on all interfaces, so it's reachable from your network. EXPOSE in a Dockerfile only documents a port; -P publishes all exposed ports to random host ports. Containers on the same network don't need port mapping to talk to each other.

terms.def: Defines a multi-container app (services, networks, volumes) in compose.yaml and starts it with one command.
terms.detail: One compose.yaml describes services (image or build, ports, env, volumes, dependencies), networks and volumes. docker compose up creates them all, in dependency order, on a private network. depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for a healthcheck, not just a started container. .env files and ${VAR} substitution keep secrets and per-machine settings out of the file. Profiles enable optional services (docker compose --profile debug up ). docker compose watch syncs code changes into containers as you edit. Great for development, CI and small single-host production. For many hosts, the same services move to Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts.

terms.def: Several FROM stages in one Dockerfile: compile in a big image, copy only the result into a small final image.
terms.detail: FROM python:3.13 AS build WORKDIR /src COPY requirements.txt. RUN pip wheel --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt FROM python:3.13-slim COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels COPY. /app USER 1000 CMD ["python", "/app/app.py"] Compilers, headers and caches stay in the build stage; only the result is copied into the final stage. For Go or .NET apps the final image can be tens of MB instead of a GB. Build a specific stage with docker build --target build. (e.g. for running tests).

terms.def: Lists files not sent to the build (.git, node_modules, .env ). Faster builds and no leaked secrets.
terms.detail: .git .venv __pycache__/ node_modules/ .env *.log dist/ Before building, Docker sends the build context (the folder) to the builder. Without a .dockerignore that includes .git history, virtual envs and secrets. Builds start faster (smaller context). COPY.. doesn't break the cache when irrelevant files change. Secrets like .env never end up in an image layer.

terms.def: The Docker daemon. It exposes the API that the CLI and Compose call, and manages images, networks and volumes.
terms.detail: The Docker daemon runs as a background service (root by default) and exposes a REST API on /var/run/docker.sock (Linux) or a named pipe (Windows). Manages images, containers, networks, volumes and builds (via BuildKit). Delegates running containers to containerd. Access to the socket = root on the host. Never mount docker.sock into untrusted containers or expose the API over TCP without TLS. Rootless mode runs the daemon as a normal user for better security; Podman avoids a daemon entirely.

terms.def: The lower-level runtimes Docker uses: containerd manages container lifecycles, runc creates the process following the OCI spec.
terms.detail: The container stack in layers: Layer Role docker CLI / Compose user interface dockerd high-level API: builds, networks, volumes containerd image pulling, storage, container lifecycle (CNCF project) runc low-level OCI runtime: sets up namespaces and cgroups, starts the process, exits Kubernetes talks to containerd directly through the CRI, skipping dockerd. That's why images built with Docker run unchanged on Kubernetes: they're standard OCI images. Alternative low-level runtimes: crun (faster), gVisor and Kata (stronger isolation).

terms.def: Linux kernel features behind containers: namespaces isolate what a process can see, cgroups limit what it can use.
terms.detail: Namespace Isolates pid process tree: the app sees itself as PID 1 net network interfaces, IPs, ports mnt filesystem mounts: the image's root filesystem uts hostname ipc shared memory, semaphores user UID mapping: root inside, unprivileged outside (rootless) cgroups limit and account resources: --memory 512m (exceed it and the kernel OOM-kills the process), --cpus 1.5 (throttled above it), PIDs and disk I/O. Seeing it yourself: docker run --rm alpine ps lists a single process, and docker stats shows each container's cgroup usage. Kubernetes requests and limits are translated into these same cgroup settings.
