sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A set of machines (nodes) plus a control plane that manages them as one big computer for containers.
terms.detail: A cluster is the unit you create, upgrade and secure. You talk to it only through its API server; the machines behind it are interchangeable. Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager. Managed services (AKS, EKS, GKE) run and patch it for you. Worker nodes: where your pods actually run. Typical sizes Setting Nodes Laptop (kind, minikube) 1–3 containers pretending to be nodes Small production 3–10 nodes Large hundreds; the documented limit is 5,000 nodes Many companies run several clusters (dev, staging, prod, per region) rather than one giant one: a smaller blast radius and easier upgrades.

terms.def: A worker machine (VM or physical) that runs pods. Each runs a kubelet, kube-proxy and a container runtime.
terms.detail: A node offers allocatable resources to pods: its total CPU and memory minus what is reserved for the OS and Kubernetes' own agents. On every node kubelet: the agent. Watches the API server for pods assigned to this node and starts or stops their containers. container runtime: usually containerd; pulls images and runs containers. kube-proxy (or a CNI like Cilium): implements Service routing on the node. Common sizes Production nodes are often 4–16 vCPU with 16–64 GiB of memory (e.g. Azure Standard_D4s_v5: 4 vCPU, 16 GiB). Several medium nodes usually beat one huge node: losing one costs less. Statuses: Ready, NotReady (kubelet stopped reporting), SchedulingDisabled (cordoned for maintenance).

terms.def: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share an IP address and volumes and are always scheduled together.
terms.detail: You almost never create pods directly; a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job creates them for you and replaces them when they die. Containers in one pod talk over localhost and can share volumes. Typical shape: one main container, optionally a sidecar (log shipper, proxy) and init containers that run first. Pods are ephemeral: a replacement gets a new name and a new IP. Reach them through a Service. Lifecycle phases Pending → Running → Succeeded / Failed. Common trouble states you'll see in kubectl get pods: ImagePullBackOff (wrong image or no registry access), CrashLoopBackOff (container keeps exiting), OOMKilled (exceeded memory limit).

terms.def: The CPU unit Kubernetes counts in: 1 CPU = one vCPU or hyperthread = 1000 millicores (1000m ).
terms.detail: A vCPU is one virtual CPU as sold by a cloud provider: usually one hyperthread of a physical core. Kubernetes measures CPU in these units and lets you ask for fractions, written in millicores: 1000m = 1 vCPU, 250m = a quarter. Common values Request Typical workload 50m–100m sidecars, small agents, idle-most-of-the-time services 250m–500m a typical web API or worker replica 1 – 2 CPU-heavy services, JVM apps at startup, build jobs 4+ databases, ML inference, batch processing A node with 4 vCPU has roughly 3.8 vCPU allocatable after system reservations. The scheduler only places a pod where the sum of requests fits. CPU on a 4-vCPU node How it relates Requests reserve vCPU for scheduling; limits cap usage. Going over the CPU limit only slows the container (throttling); going over the memory limit kills it (OOMKilled ). The HPA measures CPU usage as a percentage of the request, so a wrong request makes autoscaling wrong too. Node size in vCPU sets how many pods fit; cloud cost is mostly "vCPU × hours".

terms.def: Per-container CPU and memory settings: requests are reserved for scheduling, limits are the hard ceiling.
terms.detail: resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi } limits: { memory: 512Mi } Requests: what the scheduler adds up to decide if a pod fits on a node. Your guaranteed share. CPU limit: usage above it is throttled. Many teams set no CPU limit to avoid needless throttling, relying on requests for fairness. Memory limit: exceeding it gets the container killed (OOMKilled) and restarted. Always set one. Quality of Service classes Class When Evicted Guaranteed requests = limits for CPU and memory last Burstable requests set, lower than limits middle BestEffort nothing set first Memory units: Mi / Gi are powers of 2 (256Mi ≈ 268 MB); M / G are powers of 10.

terms.def: Declares how many replicas of a stateless pod should run and rolls out new versions gradually.
terms.detail: The workhorse object for web apps, APIs and workers. You change the image tag; the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods over. Rolling update knobs maxSurge: 25%: how many extra pods may exist during a rollout. maxUnavailable: 25%: how many may be missing. Set to 0 for zero downtime. New pods must pass their readiness probe before old ones are removed. kubectl rollout undo deployment/web switches back to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds. Kubernetes keeps 10 old revisions by default. For stateful software with stable identities (databases, Kafka brokers) use a StatefulSet instead.

terms.def: Keeps exactly N identical pods running. Deployments create and manage ReplicaSets for you.
terms.detail: A ReplicaSet runs the simplest reconcile loop: count the pods matching my label selector; create or delete pods until the count equals replicas. You rarely touch them directly. During a rollout a Deployment owns two ReplicaSets, old and new, and scales one down while scaling the other up. Their names carry the pod-template hash: web-7d9f8c, and pods are named web-7d9f8c-x2k4q. Deleting a pod by hand is safe: the ReplicaSet notices the shortfall and creates a replacement within seconds.

terms.def: A stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to the Ready pods matching a label selector.
terms.detail: Pods come and go with new IPs; a Service gives clients one address that never changes: web.shop.svc.cluster.local, or just web from the same namespace. Types Type Reachable from ClusterIP (default) inside the cluster only NodePort every node's IP on a port 30000–32767 LoadBalancer a cloud load balancer with a public or private IP Headless (clusterIP: None) DNS returns pod IPs directly (used by StatefulSets) Only pods passing their readiness probe are listed as endpoints, which is how rollouts and failures avoid sending traffic to broken pods.

terms.def: HTTP(S) routing from outside the cluster to Services by host name and path, with TLS termination.
terms.detail: Instead of one cloud load balancer per Service, a single entry point routes shop.example.com/api to the api Service and / to web. Ingress: the original API; needs an ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, cloud-specific) installed in the cluster. Gateway API: the newer, more expressive successor (traffic splitting, header matching, roles for platform vs app teams). Prefer it for new setups. TLS certificates are usually issued automatically by cert-manager with Let's Encrypt.

terms.def: A virtual folder inside a cluster for grouping and isolating objects, quotas and permissions.
terms.detail: Names must be unique only within a namespace, so team-a and team-b can both have a Service called api. Built-in: default, kube-system (cluster components), kube-public, kube-node-lease. Attach ResourceQuotas (max CPU/memory per team), RBAC roles and NetworkPolicies per namespace. Namespaces are not a security boundary by themselves: pods can still talk across them unless NetworkPolicies say otherwise. Common layouts: one namespace per team, per app, or per environment in a shared dev cluster. Select one with -n shop or set it as default for your context.

terms.def: Key/value tags on objects (app=web) and the queries that pick objects by them. The glue of Kubernetes.
terms.detail: Kubernetes rarely references objects by name. A Service, ReplicaSet or NetworkPolicy finds its pods with a selector such as app=web,tier=frontend. metadata: labels: { app: web, version: "1.4", team: shop } --- selector: matchLabels: { app: web } Recommended keys: app.kubernetes.io/name, /version, /component, /part-of. Query from the CLI: kubectl get pods -l app=web. Gotcha: a typo in a selector means a Service with zero endpoints, silently. Check with kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web.

terms.def: Configuration and credentials stored separately from the image and injected as env vars or files.
terms.detail: The same image runs in dev and prod; only its ConfigMaps and Secrets differ. ConfigMap: plain settings (feature flags, URLs, config files). Secret: passwords, tokens, TLS keys. Only base64-encoded, not encrypted, unless you enable encryption at rest. Restrict access with RBAC. Mounted as files they update in place after a short delay; as env vars they're read only at container start, so you need a rollout (kubectl rollout restart) to pick up changes. Production teams often sync secrets from a vault (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) with the External Secrets Operator.

terms.def: A pod's request for durable storage ("10Gi, read-write"), fulfilled by a PersistentVolume from a StorageClass.
terms.detail: Container filesystems disappear with the pod. A PVC asks for a disk that outlives it; the cluster provisions one dynamically (an Azure Disk, an EBS volume…) via a StorageClass. Access modes Mode Meaning Typical backend ReadWriteOnce one node mounts it read-write cloud block disks ReadWriteMany many nodes read-write NFS, Azure Files, EFS ReadOnlyMany many nodes read-only shared datasets Block disks are tied to one availability zone: a pod using one can only be rescheduled to nodes in that zone. Check the reclaimPolicy: Delete removes the disk with the claim.

terms.def: Like a Deployment, but each pod gets a stable name, stable DNS and its own persistent volume.
terms.detail: Pods are named db-0, db-1, db-2, created in order and keep their name and disk across restarts. A headless Service gives each one a DNS name like db-0.db. Used for databases, Kafka brokers, Elasticsearch, ZooKeeper-style clusters: software where members are not interchangeable. Running databases on Kubernetes is possible but demanding (backups, upgrades, failover). Operators such as CloudNativePG or Strimzi automate it; managed cloud databases are often simpler.

terms.def: Runs one copy of a pod on every node (or a chosen subset), for node-level agents.
terms.detail: When a node joins, the DaemonSet adds its pod there automatically; when it leaves, the pod goes with it. Typical uses: log collectors (Fluent Bit), metrics agents (node-exporter, Datadog agent), network plugins (Cilium), storage drivers. Use a nodeSelector or tolerations to target, say, only GPU nodes.

terms.def: Health checks the kubelet runs: liveness restarts a stuck container, readiness controls traffic, startup protects slow boots.
terms.detail: Probe If it fails… Check readiness pod removed from Service endpoints (no restart) "can I serve traffic now?" (DB connected, cache warm) liveness container is restarted "am I deadlocked?" Keep it cheap and local startup other probes wait until it passes for apps that take a minute to boot readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8000 } periodSeconds: 5 Classic mistake: a liveness probe that checks the database. When the database is slow, every pod restarts at once and turns a blip into an outage.

terms.def: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adds or removes replicas based on CPU, memory or custom metrics.
terms.detail: kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10 Every 15 s it computes desired = ceil(current × actual / target). With 3 pods at 140% of their CPU request and a 70% target, it scales to 6. Needs metrics-server and CPU requests on the pods, since utilisation is measured against them. Scales down slowly by design (5-minute stabilisation window) to avoid flapping. It adds pods, not machines: the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes when pods stay Pending. KEDA scales on queue length, Kafka lag and more.

terms.def: The package manager for Kubernetes: templated YAML bundles ("charts") installed and upgraded as releases.
terms.detail: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami helm install cache bitnami/redis -n shop --set auth.enabled=true helm upgrade cache bitnami/redis -f values-prod.yaml helm rollback cache 1 A chart is templates plus a values.yaml; you override values per environment. Helm records each install as a numbered revision you can roll back to. Alternatives: Kustomize (built into kubectl, patches plain YAML without templates) and GitOps tools like Argo CD or Flux that apply either from a Git repo.

pages.title: Percentiles
pages.tagline: The average is a number nobody experienced. Percentiles are measurements of real requests.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · the maths is permanent; the tooling notes cover Prometheus, OpenTelemetry and Azure Monitor
pages.description: Percentiles cheatsheet: p50, p90, p99 and the long tail, animated from raw samples, tail amplification under fan-out, coordinated omission, histograms, sketches and SLOs.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The value below which a given percentage of sorted measurements fall. p99 = 1.4 s means 99% of requests finished in under 1.4 seconds.
terms.detail: Sort the measurements, then read the value at the position corresponding to the percentage. Two conventions exist, and tools disagree about which they use. Method Index for p q of n samples Used by Nearest rank ceil(q/100 x n), no interpolation most monitoring tools; always a real observed value Linear interpolation interpolates between neighbours NumPy, SQL PERCENTILE_CONT, Excel samples = [38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 51, 52, 55, 62, 120, 310, 2100] # nearest rank: ceil(0.90 * 20) = 18 -> samples[17] = 120 ms The difference matters only at the extremes and with small samples, but it is enough to make two dashboards disagree about the same data. When comparing numbers across tools, check the method before concluding that something regressed. "Quantile" is the same idea expressed as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. Prometheus speaks quantiles, most dashboards speak percentiles.

terms.def: The middle measurement: half the requests were faster, half slower. The honest answer to "how fast is it normally?"
terms.detail: The median describes the typical experience and is almost completely insensitive to outliers — which makes it a good health baseline and a poor alarm. p50 tells you p50 hides whether the common path got slower everything about the worst 50% the effect of a code or query change GC pauses, cold caches, lock contention a clean signal for capacity trends that 1% of users are having a terrible time Use p50 to understand what the system normally does and the high percentiles to understand what it does when it goes wrong. A p50 that is flat while p99 triples is the classic signature of a resource that is occasionally saturated — a connection pool, a disk, a single hot partition. Watch both or you will misread both. A p50 rising while p99 stays put usually means a genuinely slower code path; a p99 rising alone usually means contention.

terms.def: The tail. p99 is the standard target for user-facing latency SLOs; p99.9 is where infrastructure problems live.
terms.detail: Each extra nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more engineering effort and exposes a different class of problem. Percentile 1 in… Usually reveals p50 2 the ordinary code path p90 10 cache misses, slightly larger payloads p95 20 cold starts, occasional lock waits p99 100 GC pauses, retries, connection churn, a hot shard p99.9 1,000 failovers, noisy neighbours, network blips p99.99 10,000 hardware faults, deployments, leap-second-class oddities Pick the percentile from the number of requests a user makes, not from fashion. A user who makes 100 requests per session touches your p99 roughly once per session, so for them p99 is not rare at all — it is the experience of a normal session. And do not track a percentile you cannot measure: p99.9 over a window containing 500 requests is noise, however confidently the dashboard draws it.

terms.def: The mean is pulled by outliers; the median is not. For long-tailed data the mean is a number almost nobody experienced.
terms.detail: In the twenty-sample set from the first animation: median 46 ms, mean 166 ms. The mean is slower than 17 of the 20 requests. Scenario Mean Median Which is right? "How fast is a typical request?" misleading correct median "How much total CPU time did we burn?" correct useless mean (it has a total) "Did the worst requests get worse?" blind blind neither — p99 "What will this cost per month?" correct wrong mean The mean is not useless; it is the only one of the two that is additive, which is exactly what you want for cost, throughput and resource consumption. It is simply the wrong summary for experience. A quick test for whether a distribution is long-tailed: if the mean is well above the median, it is. For most web latency, mean ≈ p70–p80.

terms.def: The small fraction of requests that are dramatically slower than the rest. Not noise, and not removable by averaging it away.
terms.detail: Tails are produced by mechanisms, not by randomness, which is why they are usually fixable once you can see them. Cause Signature Typical fix Garbage collection pause periodic spikes, all endpoints at once allocation reduction, GC tuning, a different collector Cold cache / cold start spikes after deploy or scale-out warm-up, pre-provisioned instances Lock or connection-pool contention p99 explodes while p50 is flat pool sizing, shorter transactions, bulkheads Retries bimodal: a cluster at roughly 2x the timeout budgeted retries, jitter, hedging A hot shard or key tail concentrated on specific inputs better key distribution, caching Noisy neighbour tail that moves between instances isolation, dedicated capacity A bimodal distribution — two humps rather than one tail — always means two code paths. Cache hit versus miss, fast path versus retry, warm versus cold. Percentiles summarise the mixture; traces tell you which path a slow request took.

terms.def: How percentiles are actually computed at scale: count observations into predefined ranges, then interpolate. Cheap, aggregatable, approximate.
terms.detail: Storing every measurement is impossible at volume, so systems store counts per bucket. The percentile is then interpolated inside whichever bucket contains the target rank. le="0.005" 12043 # 12,043 requests took Property Consequence Accuracy is bounded by bucket width a p99 landing in a 100 ms–1 s bucket is accurate to within that range Buckets are chosen in advance pick them around your SLO: if the target is 300 ms, you need a boundary at 300 ms Everything above the last bucket is +Inf if the top bucket is 1 s and your tail is 8 s, the tool reports 1 s Counters are additive histograms from many instances can be summed, then the percentile computed once — this is the whole point In Prometheus terms: histograms are aggregatable and approximate (compute percentiles at query time with histogram_quantile ); summaries compute exact percentiles per instance but cannot be combined across instances. Choose histograms unless you have exactly one instance, forever.

terms.def: Data structures — t-digest, HDR histogram, DDSketch — that give accurate percentiles in a few kilobytes, with mergeable state.
terms.detail: Fixed buckets force you to guess the range in advance. Sketches adapt, and most of them are mergeable, which solves the aggregation problem properly. Structure Guarantee Good for HDR histogram configurable relative error, fixed memory load testing, latency recording in-process t-digest very accurate at the extremes, less so in the middle exactly the shape of a latency problem DDSketch guaranteed relative error at every quantile SLO reporting where the bound must be provable Fixed buckets error bounded by bucket width Prometheus; simple and good enough with sensible boundaries The property that matters is mergeability: a sketch per instance per minute can be merged into a sketch for the whole fleet per hour, and the percentile read from that. No averaging of percentiles, no loss of the tail. Relative error is the right guarantee for latency, because being 5% wrong about 20 ms and 5% wrong about 5 s are both fine, whereas a fixed absolute error is either useless at the bottom or enormous at the top.

terms.def: You cannot average p99s across instances, regions or time windows. The result is not a percentile of anything.
terms.detail: The single most common mistake in monitoring, and most dashboards make it by default when a query groups by instance and then averages. A counterexample Requests p99 Instance A (healthy) 990,000 50 ms Instance B (sick) 10,000 5,000 ms Average of the two p99s — 2,525 ms — nonsense True fleet p99 1,000,000 ~55 ms The average suggests the whole fleet is catastrophically slow; the truth is that 1% of traffic is. Reverse the request counts and the average is equally wrong in the other direction. The fix is always the same: aggregate the raw distributions — sum the histogram buckets, merge the sketches — and compute the percentile once over the total. # right: sum the buckets, then take the quantile histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # wrong: a quantile per instance, then averaged avg(histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) The same applies over time: a p99 for a day is not the mean of 24 hourly p99s. You need the day's distribution.

terms.def: A percentile is always "over what period". Change the window and you change the number, sometimes by a lot.
terms.detail: p99 over one minute answers "how bad was the worst minute"; p99 over a month answers "how bad is the service". They are different questions and will give different numbers. Window Behaviour Use for 1 minute noisy, reacts instantly alerting on a sudden regression 5–15 minutes the usual dashboard compromise day-to-day operations 1 hour smooth, hides short spikes trends, capacity 28–30 days the SLO window error budgets and commitments A short window on a low-traffic endpoint is a trap: ten requests a minute means a one-minute p99 is simply the slowest of ten, and it will jump around wildly without anything changing. State the window everywhere. "p99 is 400 ms" is not a fact; "p99 over the last 7 days is 400 ms" is.

terms.def: You need roughly 100 samples to see p99 at all, and far more for it to be stable. Below that the number is theatre.
terms.detail: A percentile is a position in a sorted list, so with n samples the finest resolution you have is 1/ n. Samples in the window Finest meaningful percentile Comment 20 p95 "p99" is just the maximum 100 p99 one single sample defines it — very noisy 1,000 p99 (stable-ish), p99.9 visible a reasonable minimum for alerting 100,000 p99.9 solid, p99.99 visible comfortable Rule of thumb: you want at least 10 samples beyond the percentile you are reporting, so p99 needs about 1,000 requests in the window and p99.9 about 10,000. When traffic is low, widen the window instead of lowering the standard — and be honest on the dashboard: an "insufficient data" panel is worth more than a confident wrong number.

terms.def: When one user action depends on many calls, the probability of hitting the tail multiplies. Fan-out turns a rare event into a common one.
terms.detail: If each of n independent calls is fast with probability p, all of them are fast with probability p n. Calls per request P(at least one in the p99 tail) 1 1% 5 4.9% 10 9.6% 50 39.5% 100 63.4% So a microservice architecture with heavy fan-out inherits a far worse tail than any of its parts, and every team's dashboard can look fine while the page is slow. This is the core argument of Google's The Tail at Scale. Three defences, in order of preference: reduce fan-out (batch calls, denormalise, cache), make the tail shorter at the source, and tolerate it with hedging and timeouts. Measuring end to end, from the user's point of view, is what tells you whether you need any of them.

terms.def: A measurement bug where the tool stops sending requests while the system is stalled, so the queueing delay every real user felt is never recorded.
terms.detail: Named by Gil Tene. It makes load-test results optimistic by an order of magnitude or more, and it is the default behaviour of most naive benchmark harnesses. The same stall, measured two ways The giveaway in a report is a p99 that is close to the p50 while the maximum is enormous. Real systems under load have a smooth climb from p50 to p99; a flat line with a cliff at the top means the queueing was never measured.

terms.def: Techniques that make a slow request stop mattering: hedging, timeouts with degradation, and reducing how much depends on how much.
terms.detail: You cannot eliminate a tail — shared infrastructure guarantees one — so the practical goal is to make it not reach the user. Technique How Cost Hedged request after p95 has elapsed, send a duplicate and take whichever answers first ~5% extra load for a large p99 improvement Tied request send to two replicas, each cancels the other on start needs cooperation between replicas Timeout + degrade drop the recommendations panel after 100 ms a slightly poorer page instead of a slow one Reduce fan-out batch, denormalise, cache design work; the most durable fix Micro-partitioning many small shards, rebalanced away from slow nodes operational complexity Hedging only works if requests are idempotent and the extra load is affordable. Set the hedge delay at the p95, not the p50, or you double your traffic for nothing. The cheapest tail tolerance is usually a timeout plus a default. Deciding in advance what the page looks like without the slow component is design work, not infrastructure work.

terms.def: An indicator is what you measure; an objective is the target. Latency SLOs are almost always expressed as a percentile over a window.
terms.detail: A well-formed latency SLO names the percentile, the threshold, the window and the scope. 99% of GET /orders/{id} requests complete in under 300 ms, measured at the gateway, over a rolling 28-day window. Part Why it must be stated Percentile and threshold "fast" is not measurable Window a 1-minute p99 and a 28-day p99 are different numbers Measurement point client, edge, gateway and service all see different latencies Scope one endpoint, not an average over all of them The common alternative formulation is a threshold SLO: "99% of requests under 300 ms" counted as good-event / total-event. It is easier to reason about and to combine than a percentile value, which is why Google's SRE practice leans on it — and it is also what makes an error budget straightforward to compute. Set the target from what users need, then check it against what the system does. An SLO you already meet with no effort measures nothing; one you miss every week is a wish.

terms.def: The amount of failure the SLO permits. 99.9% over 30 days is 43 minutes of budget, and spending it is allowed.
terms.detail: The budget turns reliability from an argument into arithmetic: if the budget is intact you may ship; if it is spent you fix reliability first. Objective Budget per 30 days Per week 99% 7h 12m 1h 41m 99.5% 3h 36m 50m 99.9% 43m 12s 10m 5s 99.95% 21m 36s 5m 2s 99.99% 4m 19s 1m A latency SLO consumes budget the same way: every request slower than the threshold is a bad event. That is why the threshold formulation is easier to operate than a percentile value — you can count bad events, but you cannot count "p99 was 310 ms". Alert on burn rate, not on the current value. A page at 2am is justified by "we are consuming the month's budget 14 times faster than sustainable", not by a p99 that crossed a line for 60 seconds.

terms.def: p99 = 1.4 s does not mean "99% as good" or "1% of requests failed". It is a position in a sorted list, not a proportion of anything.
terms.detail: The confusion is common enough in meetings to be worth naming explicitly. Statement Correct? "p99 is 1.4 s" = 99% of requests took 1.4 s or less yes "p99 is 1.4 s" = 1% of requests failed no — they were slow, not failed "We improved p99 by 10%" is a clear statement ambiguous — the value, or the position? "99th percentile" and "top 1%" describe the same requests yes Also beware the word "percentile" applied to things that are not latency without saying which direction is good. For response sizes or error counts, a high percentile is the big one; for throughput or scores, a high percentile is the good one. Say which you mean.

terms.def: Dropping the extreme values before averaging. Useful for benchmarking noise, dangerous for production monitoring.
terms.detail: A trimmed mean discards the top and bottom x % and averages the rest, giving a stable central estimate that is not thrown by a single outlier. Use it for Do not use it for benchmark runs where one result was a background job production latency — you are deleting your incidents comparing two implementations in a noisy environment SLO reporting of any kind estimating a central tendency in dirty data anything where the extremes are the question The rule: trimming is legitimate when outliers are measurement artefacts, and illegitimate when they are real user experiences. In production they are almost always real. Before deleting an outlier, trace it. "A 9-second request" is not noise — it is a lead, and usually the most informative one you have that day.

pages.title: Rate limiting
pages.tagline: Say no on purpose, before the system says no by falling over.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · the algorithms are stable; only the implementations move
pages.description: Rate limiting cheatsheet: fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket and GCRA, with animated walk-throughs, distributed counters, headers and gotchas.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The policy itself: N requests per unit of time, e.g. 100 / minute. Everything else is how you measure the window.
terms.detail: A limit is a pair: a count and a period. The period is what makes the algorithms differ — a minute measured from the clock behaves very differently from a minute measured backwards from now. Common values Surface Typical limit Keyed on Public read API 60–1,000 / min API key Login / password reset 5–10 / 15 min account + IP Expensive report endpoint 5–20 / hour tenant Outbound call to a partner their published limit minus 10% your whole fleet SMS / email send 1 / min, 10 / day phone or address Pick limits from measured capacity, not from a round number: load-test one instance, divide by the number of tenants you must serve concurrently, then leave headroom. Publish the limit in your docs and in response headers — an undocumented limit is indistinguishable from an outage.

terms.def: What you count per: API key, user id, tenant, IP, endpoint, or a combination. Choosing it wrong is the most common design mistake.
terms.detail: The key decides who suffers when the limit bites. A key that is too broad punishes innocent callers; a key that is too narrow is trivially bypassed. Key Good for Weakness ip anonymous traffic, scrapers NAT and CGNAT share one IP; IPv6 hands an attacker a whole /64 api-key / tenant paid APIs, fairness between customers useless before authentication user-id abuse of a feature by one account new accounts are cheap tenant + route protecting one expensive endpoint many counters to manage account and ip (both) credential stuffing needs two checks per request Compose the key as a string you can read in a dump: rl:{tenant:acme}:POST:/reports:10:05. In Redis Cluster, wrap the part that must stay on one node in braces so a multi-key script still works. Layer keys rather than choosing one: a coarse IP limit at the edge, a precise tenant limit in the app.

terms.def: One counter per clock period: INCR a key named after the current minute, reject above the limit, let it expire. The cheapest correct-ish option.
terms.detail: Two operations per request and one key per active caller per period. The key name is the window, so expiry does the cleanup for you. key = f"rl:{user}:{int(time.time() // 60)}" n = r.incr(key) if n == 1: r.expire(key, 120) allowed = n <= limit Cost and accuracy Property Value Memory per caller ~1 small key (60–100 B) Ops per request 1–2 (INCR, sometimes EXPIRE) Worst-case burst 2x the limit, across the boundary Fairness poor: whoever arrives first in the window wins The boundary burst (see the first animation) is not theoretical: clients that retry on a schedule all align to the start of the minute, so you get a thundering herd at :00 every minute. Add jitter on the client, or move to a sliding window. Use it when the limit is generous and the cost of 2x is acceptable — which covers most internal APIs.

terms.def: Store the timestamp of every request, drop the ones older than the window, count what is left. Exact, and the most expensive.
terms.detail: Keep a sorted set per caller, scored by timestamp. On each request: remove entries older than now − window, count, add the new entry if under the limit. ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:acme 0 (now-60000) ZCARD rl:acme -- how many in the last 60 s ZADD rl:acme now now:req-id -- only if under the limit EXPIRE rl:acme 60 Cost Property Value Memory per caller limit x 50–80 B (a 10,000/min limit is ~700 KB per key) Ops per request 3–4, best run as one Lua script Accuracy exact — never more than the limit in any 60 s Perfect accuracy is rarely worth the memory. Reserve it for small, high-value limits where every single call matters: login attempts, one-time-code sends, payment submissions, free-tier trial calls.

terms.def: Two fixed windows, weighted: prev x overlap + current. Nearly as accurate as the log, at the cost of a fixed window.
terms.detail: Keep the current window's counter and the previous one's. Estimate the count over the trailing window by assuming the previous window's requests were spread evenly through it. elapsed = now % 60 # seconds into the current minute overlap = (60 - elapsed) / 60 # how much of prev is still in range estimate = prev * overlap + current allowed = estimate < limit Worked example Moment prev curr estimate Verdict 10:01:02 (2 s in) 5 5 5 x 0.97 + 5 = 9.85 reject 10:01:30 (30 s in) 5 2 5 x 0.50 + 2 = 4.50 allow 10:01:55 (55 s in) 5 4 5 x 0.08 + 4 = 4.42 allow The estimate is wrong only when the previous window's traffic was very unevenly distributed, and it errs on the strict side for the pattern that matters (a burst at the end of the previous window). Cloudflare published measurements showing well under 1% misclassification at scale. This is the default worth reaching for.

terms.def: A bucket refills at a constant rate up to a capacity; each request spends one token. Capacity sets the burst, refill rate sets the sustained rate.
terms.detail: The two knobs map directly onto the two things you actually care about, which is why this is the algorithm most public APIs use. Knob Controls Typical capacity largest burst allowed after idling 1–10x the per-second rate refill rate long-run sustained throughput the published limit divided by the period cost per request weighting expensive calls 1 normally; 10 for a report; 0 for a health check You do not run a timer. Store (tokens, last_refill) and compute lazily on each request: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now − last_refill) x rate). Two fields, one key, O(1). Variable cost is the quiet superpower: charge a search 1 token and a bulk export 50, and a single limit then expresses "work per second" rather than "calls per second". Most cloud APIs are token buckets underneath.

terms.def: Arrivals queue in a bucket that drains at a fixed rate; overflow is dropped. Output is perfectly smooth, at the price of added latency.
terms.detail: Two variants share the name. The queue form (below) actually holds requests and releases them at a constant rate — traffic shaping. The meter form holds only a level that drains over time and rejects immediately when full, which is mathematically the mirror image of a token bucket and what most libraries mean. Form On excess Equivalent to Queue (shaping) delays the request; drops only when the queue is full nothing else here — it trades errors for latency Meter (level that drains) rejects immediately the mirror image of a token bucket: level up instead of tokens down Animation 5 in "How it works" walks the queueing form through the same nine requests the other algorithms saw — it is the only one that rejected nothing and the only one that added 56 seconds of latency. Use the queueing form when the downstream is the thing you are protecting and a little latency is cheaper than a rejection — writing to a legacy ERP, calling a partner with a hard contractual rate. Use the metering form for ordinary API limits, where it is simply a token bucket with the arithmetic inverted.

terms.def: Generic Cell Rate Algorithm: a leaky bucket stored as a single timestamp, the "theoretical arrival time". One field, exact, no boundary burst.
terms.detail: Borrowed from ATM networking. Instead of a level that decays, store the theoretical arrival time (TAT) of the next permitted request. With an emission interval T = period / limit and a burst tolerance tau = (burst − 1) x T: if now < tat - tau: reject, retry after (tat - tau) - now else: tat = max(now, tat) + T; allow Why it is nice One value per key instead of a counter plus a timestamp: a single GET / SET, trivially atomic. It yields the exact retry-after for free, which a counter cannot give you. There is no window boundary at all, so there is no boundary burst. This is what redis-cell (CL.THROTTLE) implements, and what several Go and Rust limiters use. The maths is unfamiliar at first glance; the implementation is four lines.

terms.def: How far above the sustained rate a caller may go for a short time. Some burst is a feature: it absorbs page loads that fire ten calls at once.
terms.detail: Real clients are bursty by nature: one page render fans out into a dozen API calls. A limiter with zero burst tolerance rejects correct, well-behaved traffic. Algorithm Burst you get Fixed window up to 2x the limit, accidentally, at the boundary Sliding window counter slightly over the limit, bounded Sliding window log none — exactly the limit Token bucket exactly the capacity, deliberately Leaky bucket (queue) none in the output; the queue absorbs it as latency GCRA exactly tau, deliberately Rule of thumb: set burst to the number of calls one user action legitimately produces, usually 5–20. Deliberate burst in a token bucket is safe; accidental burst in a fixed window is not, because it clusters on the clock across all your callers at once.

terms.def: The HTTP contract: status 429, a Retry-After header in seconds, and RateLimit-* headers so clients can self-regulate before being rejected.
terms.detail: A rejection that does not say when to come back forces clients to guess, and they guess badly. The IETF RateLimit header fields give a standard shape: HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: 7 RateLimit-Limit: 100 RateLimit-Remaining: 0 RateLimit-Reset: 7 Status Means Client should 429 you exceeded your limit back off, retry after the hint 503 + Retry-After the service is overloaded back off harder: the whole fleet is affected 403 never allowed stop, do not retry Send RateLimit-Remaining on successful responses too — that is what lets a well-written client slow down before it hits the wall. And keep the 429 body small and uncached: rejections should be the cheapest response you produce.

terms.def: With n instances behind a load balancer the counter must be shared and the check must be atomic, usually one Redis round trip running a Lua script.
terms.detail: Read-then-write across the network is a race: two instances both read 99, both allow, and a limit of 100 passes 101. The check and the increment must be one operation. -- token bucket, atomic, one round trip local t = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts') local now, rate, cap = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3]) local tokens = math.min(cap, (tonumber(t[1]) or cap) + (now - (tonumber(t[2]) or now)) * rate) if tokens < 1 then return {0, math.ceil((1 - tokens) / rate)} end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens - 1, 'ts', now) redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate) + 1) return {1, 0} Budget it Concern Guidance Added latency 0.3–1 ms per request on a same-zone Redis Clock source use redis.call('TIME') or one server clock — never each app server's own Store is down decide fail-open or fail-closed in advance, with a tight timeout (5–20 ms) Hot key one global limit is one key on one node; shard it or limit per tenant Redis is the usual store because INCR, Lua and EXPIRE are exactly the primitives needed, and single-threaded execution makes each script atomic for free.

terms.def: Count per instance (fast, approximate, drifts with autoscaling) or in a shared store (exact, adds a network hop). Many systems do both.
terms.detail: Dividing a global limit by the instance count is tempting and usually wrong: load balancers are not perfectly even, and the divisor changes every time Kubernetes scales the deployment. Approach Latency Accuracy Use when Per-instance, limit / n 0 ms poor under uneven balancing coarse protection, huge limits Central store per request +0.3–1 ms exact paid quotas, small limits Local bucket + periodic sync ~0 ms good, bounded drift very high RPS, limits in the thousands The hybrid is how large gateways do it: each instance holds a local allowance, spends from it with no network call, and reconciles with the shared store every few hundred milliseconds. You trade a bounded overshoot for zero added latency on the hot path.

terms.def: Capping requests in flight with a semaphore rather than requests per second. Often the limit that actually protects you.
terms.detail: Rate and concurrency are different failure modes. 100 requests per second that each take 10 ms is 1 concurrent request; 100 per second that each take 2 s is 200 — and 200 threads, 200 connections, 200 open transactions. Limit type Protects against Tool Requests / second abuse, cost, fairness token bucket, sliding window Concurrent requests thread and connection exhaustion, slow dependencies semaphore, bulkhead Queue depth + timeout unbounded latency under overload bounded queue, shed on full Little's Law ties them together: concurrency = rate x latency. If your dependency slows from 50 ms to 500 ms, the same request rate produces ten times the concurrency — which is why a service with only a rate limit still dies when its database gets slow. Set both.

terms.def: Dropping work when the system itself is in trouble, regardless of whose quota it is. A rate limit is a contract; shedding is survival.
terms.detail: Quota limits are static and per-caller. Load shedding is dynamic and global: it reacts to your health signals — queue depth, p99 latency, CPU, pool saturation — and rejects whatever keeps the service alive. Priority-aware: shed background sync and analytics before interactive traffic. Tag requests with a criticality on the way in. Shed early: rejecting at the front door costs microseconds; rejecting after the database call has already cost you the database call. Drop the oldest: a request that has waited 5 s probably belongs to a client that already timed out. Under overload, LIFO sheds better than FIFO. Signal it with 503 and Retry-After, not 429: the caller did nothing wrong, and the distinction tells their on-call engineer where the problem actually is.

terms.def: Pushing the "slow down" signal upstream instead of silently queueing. A bounded queue that blocks the producer is backpressure; an unbounded one is a time bomb.
terms.detail: Every unbounded buffer turns an overload into a latency disaster: memory grows, requests sit behind work nobody is waiting for any more, and recovery takes longer than the incident. Bound every queue, and decide what happens when it is full: block the producer, drop the newest, or drop the oldest. Give every queued item a deadline and discard it when the deadline passes, rather than serving a response nobody will read. In a pull-based system — a consumer group reading from Apache Kafka, or a job queue — backpressure is automatic: the consumer simply fetches more slowly and the broker holds the backlog. A rate limiter is backpressure made explicit at an HTTP boundary, where no protocol-level mechanism exists.

terms.def: Randomness added to retry delays and to window or cache expiry so that clients do not all come back at the same instant.
terms.detail: Without jitter, a limiter creates the herd it is meant to prevent: every rejected client is told the same reset time, sleeps the same number of seconds, and returns in the same millisecond. // exponential backoff with full jitter delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)) Strategy Spread Verdict Fixed delay none synchronises the herd Exponential, no jitter none still synchronised, just later Exponential + full jitter excellent the sane default Decorrelated jitter excellent better throughput during long outages Cap the total attempts and respect Retry-After when it is present. Retries that ignore a 429 are the single most effective way to turn a small limit breach into an outage.

pages.tagline: An in-memory data structure server: a key-value store that answers in microseconds.

pages.description: Redis cheatsheet: architecture, animated SET and cache-aside walk-throughs, key concepts, commands, trade-offs and alternatives.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A binary-safe string that names a value, by convention namespaced with colons: user:1, cart:7. Max 512 MB, but keep keys short.
terms.detail: Keys are binary-safe strings. Redis has no tables or schemas, so the naming convention is your schema: object-type:id:field. Good Why user:1042 type + id, easy to SCAN MATCH user:* session:9f3c short, unique, set a TTL rl:{user:42}:2026-11-10T10:05 rate-limit bucket; {…} is a Cluster hash tag Keep keys short: with 100M keys, every extra 20 bytes is ~2 GB of RAM. Avoid unbounded patterns (one key per request) without a TTL.

terms.def: The set of all keys in a database, stored in one big in-memory hash table. Lookups are O(1).
terms.detail: All keys of a database live in one big hash table, so GET, SET and DEL are O(1) whatever the size. Redis grows the table incrementally (rehashing a little on each command) to avoid long pauses. DBSIZE counts keys; INFO keyspace shows keys and expiring keys per database. Redis has 16 numbered databases (SELECT 0..15 ), but Cluster supports only db 0. Prefer key prefixes over database numbers. Scale: tens of millions of keys per instance are normal; the limit is RAM, not count.

terms.def: What a key holds: String, Hash, List, Set, Sorted set, Stream, Bitmap, HyperLogLog, Geo, JSON, Vector set. Each has its own commands.
terms.detail: Type Think of it as Typical use String bytes, number, JSON blob (≤ 512 MB) cache entries, counters, locks Hash a small object / dict user profile, session fields List linked list, push/pop at both ends queues, recent-items feeds Set unique unordered members tags, "who liked this" Sorted set members ordered by score leaderboards, scheduling, sliding windows Stream append-only log with consumer groups event streams, job queues with acks JSON, Vector set, HyperLogLog, Bitmap, Geo specialised structures documents, similarity search, unique counts, flags, "nearby" Pick the type by the operations you need: if you'd read-modify-write a JSON string to change one field, use a Hash instead.

terms.def: A time-to-live on a key. When it runs out, Redis deletes the key. The basis of caching and sessions.
terms.detail: SET session:9f "{...}" EX 1800 # set with 30 min TTL EXPIRE cart:7 3600 # add/replace a TTL TTL cart:7 → 3597 # seconds left (-1 none, -2 missing) PERSIST cart:7 # remove the TTL Expired keys are removed two ways: lazily when someone touches them, and actively by a background job that samples keys with TTLs several times per second. Memory is therefore reclaimed slightly after expiry, not at the exact second. Common values Cache entries: 1–60 min, with random jitter to avoid stampedes. Sessions: 30 min to 24 h, refreshed on activity. One-time codes: 5–10 min. Gotcha: SET without EX / KEEPTTL on an existing key removes its TTL.

terms.def: The RAM cap. When it is reached, the maxmemory-policy decides what to drop (e.g. allkeys-lru) or to reject writes (noeviction ).
terms.detail: maxmemory caps the RAM Redis uses for data. When a write would exceed it, maxmemory-policy decides what happens. Policy Evicts Use for noeviction (default) nothing: writes fail with OOM data you can't lose (queues, primary data) allkeys-lru least recently used key pure caches (most common) allkeys-lfu least frequently used key caches with stable "hot" keys volatile-lru / volatile-ttl only keys with a TTL mixed cache + persistent data allkeys-lru in action Size it: set maxmemory to ~70–80% of the machine's RAM to leave room for fragmentation, replication buffers and fork during RDB saves.

terms.def: Commands run one at a time on the main thread, so a single command like INCR never races with another.
terms.detail: Commands execute one at a time on the main thread, so INCR, SET NX, LPUSH or ZINCRBY can never interleave with another client's command. Two app servers incrementing the same counter never lose an update. But a sequence of commands from your app is not atomic: between your GET and SET another client can sneak in. Options: A single command that does it all (INCR, SET … NX GET, GETDEL ). MULTI/EXEC with WATCH for optimistic locking. A Lua script or Function: the whole script runs atomically. Since Redis 6, network I/O can use extra threads, but command execution stays single-threaded, so atomicity is unchanged.

terms.def: Send many commands without waiting for each reply. Cuts network round trips; usually the biggest client-side speedup.
terms.detail: Without pipelining each command waits for its reply: 1,000 commands × 0.5 ms round trip = 0.5 s, mostly waiting on the network. With a pipeline you send all 1,000, then read 1,000 replies: a few milliseconds. pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=False) for uid in user_ids: pipe.hgetall(f"user:{uid}") profiles = pipe.execute() Pipelining is a client-side batching trick, not a transaction: other clients' commands can still run in between. Keep batches to a few thousand commands to bound memory.

terms.def: A transaction: queued commands run together with nothing interleaved. There is no rollback if one fails.
terms.detail: WATCH stock:42 GET stock:42 → "3" MULTI DECR stock:42 LPUSH orders "…" EXEC → nil if stock:42 changed since WATCH Commands are queued and run back-to-back with nothing interleaved. No rollback: if one command fails at runtime (wrong type), the others still apply. WATCH gives optimistic locking: EXEC aborts if a watched key changed; retry in a loop. In Cluster all keys must share a hash slot. For logic with conditions ("decrement only if > 0"), a Lua script is simpler than WATCH retries.

terms.def: Server-side scripts that run atomically. Use them for read-modify-write logic, such as rate limiters.
terms.detail: A script runs entirely on the server, atomically, so it can read, decide and write in one step. Classic fixed-window rate limiter: -- KEYS[1] = rl:{user:42}:minute, ARGV[1] = limit local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60) end return n <= tonumber(ARGV[1]) EVAL sends the script each time; EVALSHA reuses a cached one. Redis 7+ Functions (FUNCTION LOAD, FCALL) store named scripts in the server and persist them with the data. Keep scripts short: while one runs, every other client waits.

terms.def: Point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset to disk. Compact and fast to load, but you lose writes made since the last snapshot.
terms.detail: Redis forks; the child writes the whole dataset to dump.rdb while the parent keeps serving. Fork uses copy-on-write, so memory use can briefly grow under heavy writes. save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000 # snapshot after N changes in T seconds BGSAVE # snapshot now LASTSAVE # when was the last one Pros: compact file, fast restarts, perfect for backups (copy it to object storage). Cons: a crash loses every write since the last snapshot, often minutes. Replicas also bootstrap from an RDB sent by the primary.

terms.def: Append-only file: every write command is logged. With appendfsync everysec, at most about 1 second of writes is lost on a crash.
terms.detail: The append-only file logs every write command; on restart Redis replays it. appendfsync Data at risk on crash Speed always ~none slow (fsync per write) everysec (default) ~1 second fast, the usual choice no up to ~30 s (OS decides) fastest The log is rewritten in the background to stay compact. Modern Redis uses a multi-part AOF with an RDB base plus incremental files. Common production setup: AOF everysec + periodic RDB for backups.

terms.def: Replicas keep an asynchronous copy of a primary. They serve reads and can be promoted if the primary fails.
terms.detail: A replica connects to the primary (REPLICAOF host 6379 ), receives an RDB snapshot, then a continuous stream of write commands. Asynchronous: the primary acknowledges the client before replicas have the write. A failover can lose the last few writes. WAIT 1 100 blocks until 1 replica has it (still not a guarantee). Replicas are read-only and can serve reads, but may lag a few ms behind. Typical setup: 1 primary + 1–2 replicas in different availability zones. Replication alone doesn't fail over automatically: that's Sentinel's or Cluster's job.

terms.def: Processes that monitor a primary and its replicas, run automatic failover and tell clients the new primary's address.
terms.detail: Sentinel is a separate process (run at least 3, on different machines) that watches a primary and its replicas. Sentinels ping the primary; if a quorum (e.g. 2 of 3) agrees it's down, they elect a leader Sentinel. The leader promotes the most up-to-date replica and reconfigures the others. Clients ask Sentinel "who is the primary for mymaster ?" and reconnect. Use Sentinel when data fits on one machine and you need automatic failover. If you need to shard data across machines, use Cluster instead; it has failover built in. Managed services (ElastiCache, Azure Cache) handle this for you.

terms.def: Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384 ). {tags} in a key force related keys into the same slot.
terms.detail: Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots: slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. Each primary owns a range of slots; each primary has replicas for failover. Node Slots A 0 – 5460 B 5461 – 10922 C 10923 – 16383 Clients cache the slot map; a MOVED reply tells them the map changed. Multi-key commands (MGET, MULTI, Lua) need all keys in one slot. Force it with a hash tag: only {user:42} is hashed in cart:{user:42} and profile:{user:42}. Resharding moves slots between nodes online.

terms.def: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget broadcast. Streams are a persistent, append-only log with consumer groups and acknowledgements.
terms.detail: Pub/Sub Streams Storage none: delivered and forgotten kept in a log (trim with MAXLEN) Offline consumers miss messages catch up from their last ID Load balancing every subscriber gets every message consumer groups split the work Acks / retries no XACK, pending list, XCLAIM Use for live notifications, cache invalidation, chat presence job queues, event sourcing, activity feeds Streams look a lot like a mini Kafka: IDs like 1731234567890-0 are timestamp-based offsets. For days of retention or very high volume, use Kafka itself.
